metadata.title: Mastoid Surgery Does Not Normalize Tympanometric Middle Ear Pressure in Children With Cholesteatoma

sections.text: ABSTRACT Objective To determine whether transcanal surgery without mastoidectomy, canal wall up (CWU), canal wall down (CWD), or CWU mastoid obliteration (MO) surgery for pediatric cholesteatoma has a more favorable effect on middle ear pressure (MEP) homeostasis. Methods Data from children having mastoid surgery for acquired cholesteatoma were collected prospectively. Tympanometric values of MEP were compared after transcanal, CWU, CWD, and MO surgery analyzing (i) a single measure per ear from last clinic visit, and (ii) linear mixed‐effects modeling (LMEM) to control for multiple measures, surgeries, age, and cholesteatoma severity (EAONO‐JOS stage). Results 742 surgeries on 471 ears and 2382 tympanograms were completed. At last visit, (average age 15.6 years [6.0–19.3]), Type a tympanograms were present in 80/173 (46%) of transcanal surgeries, 64/132 (48%) CWU, 15/32 (47%) CWD, and 11/25 (44%) MO (Chi‐square, p = 0.19), but 185/209 (89%) contralateral ears without cholesteatoma (Chi‐square: p = 1.08 × 10 −7 ). Median MEP was −47 daPa (IQR: 133) after transcanal, −65 daPa (IQR: 156) after CWU, −90 daPa (IQR: 151) after CWD, and −31 daPa (IQR: 151) after MO surgery and (Kruskal–Wallis: p = 0.4) but 5 daPa (IQR: 45) in normal contralateral ears (Wilcoxon: p = 7.92 × 10 −13 ). LMEM showed MEP was dependent on age ( p = 6.3 × 10 −7 ) but not type of mastoid surgery ( p = 0.70) or EAONO‐JOS stage ( p = 0.51). Conclusion MEP after surgery for pediatric cholesteatoma is similar after transcanal, CWU, CWD, or MO surgery and remains lower than normal. Hypotheses that propose beneficial effects of these different surgical approaches on MEP homeostasis are not supported, so should not be used to influence choice of surgical approach. Level of Evidence 3.

With stable atmospheric pressure and an intact tympanic membrane, middle ear pressure (MEP) homeostasis is maintained by passage of air up the Eustachian tube to balance absorption of gases across tympanomastoid mucosa. Without Eustachian tube opening, MEP becomes lower than atmospheric pressure [ 1 ]. This can contribute to tympanic membrane retraction and acquired cholesteatoma. Mucosal barriers to ventilation [ 2 ] and chronic sniffing with patulous Eustachian tube function [ 3 ] may also contribute. Conflicting hypotheses have been proposed that recommend different surgical approaches to normalize post‐operative MEP and prevent recurrent cholesteatoma. For example, on the basis that restoration of normal mastoid mucosal function might normalize MEP [ 4 ], transcanal surgery with opening of tympanomastoid ventilation pathways and preservation of the mastoid and its mucosa has been proposed [ 2 , 5 ]. In contrast, canal wall up tympanomastoidectomy (CWU) removes mastoid mucosa to create a larger air reservoir, potentially buffering MEP changes [ 6 ]. Paradoxically, elimination of the mastoid by canal wall down tympanomastoidectomy (CWD), or mastoid obliteration, removes the mastoid space. This removes mastoid mucosa but creates a smaller air space to facilitate MEP homeostasis [ 7 ]. With the objective of evaluating these contradictory hypotheses and the effect of different surgical approaches on MEP homeostasis, this study compares tympanometric measurements of MEP after mastoid‐sparing surgery, CWU tympanomastoidectomy, CWD tympanomastoidectomy, and CWU with mastoid obliteration in children with cholesteatoma. Linear mixed effects modeling is used to control for increasing MEP with age [ 8 ] and confounding from more invasive surgery for severe cholesteatoma.

Ethical approval for this study was provided by the institution's research ethics board. Study participants with new onset of primary acquired retraction cholesteatoma were identified and data extracted from a prospectively single‐surgeon database of 945 consecutive surgeries for cholesteatoma in children under 18 years of age maintained from 2002 to 2024. Cases of congenital, secondary acquired, ear canal cholesteatoma and those of uncertain origin were excluded [ 9 ]. Cases recorded as pre‐cholesteatoma (retraction pockets with removable keratin) were also excluded. To avoid double‐counting of results from children with bilateral cholesteatoma, only the first‐operated ear was included. Two ears having blind sac closure were excluded. Demographic data, extent of cholesteatoma (EAONO‐JOS stage, Supplement 1 ) [ 9 ], surgical approach and tympanometric MEP data were extracted for analysis.
Allocation to different surgeries was based upon pre‐ and intra‐operative findings of extent of cholesteatoma. Four surgical categories were defined by mastoid management.

Mastoid‐sparing surgery: when not extending beyond the lateral semicircular canal, cholesteatoma was removed without mastoid surgery, via a post‐auricular incision or endoscopically trans‐canal. Atticotomy was reconstructed with cartilage scutumplasty (A1 or A4, M2a or M2b, E2, Ox using SAMEO‐ATO nomenclature, Supplement 1 [ 10 ]). The tympanic isthmus was opened in all cases to allow tympanomastoid ventilation. Mastoid mucosal surface area is preserved with this approach.

Canal wall up tympanomastoidectomy (CWU): cholesteatoma extending into the mastoid beyond the reach of transcanal approach was managed with a cortical mastoidectomy drilled to the limit of the size of the cholesteatoma, often supplemented by an atticotomy with scutumplasty to keep the canal wall intact (A4, M1a or M1b ± M2a, E2, Ox). Mastoid volume was increased by this approach and some mucosa preserved if not involved with cholesteatoma. Of note, previous analysis of a subset of these patients showed the mastoid only remains well‐ventilated in around half of these cases [ 11 ].

Canal wall down tympanomastoidectomy (CWD) (A4, M2bE1 or M2cE1 with Ox, O1 or O2). CWD was initially offered as a single‐stage option, but given the requirement for revisions in children, the worse hearing outcomes, and the challenges of cavity management, it was used less commonly in recent years for children with a small mastoid and narrow ear canal [ 12 , 13 ]. Mastoid obliteration with bone paté and soft tissue rotation flap was added to most CWD surgeries to reduce cavity size and care issues. In the CWD approach, the mastoid air space is externalized (whether obliterated or not) so it does not contribute to MEP homeostasis.

Mastoid obliteration with the CWU bony obliteration technique (BOT) [ 14 ] (A4 M1a or M1b with or without M2a, Ex, O2) was used with bone paté for aggressive or recurrent cholesteatoma. After BOT, as in Group C, MEP influence is eliminated but middle ear volume may be slightly larger as the tympanic membrane is medialized down to the facial nerve in Group C. Surgery was repeated as needed as a planned staged procedure to check for residual disease, because of presence of recurrent cholesteatoma or for elective ossiculoplasty, and allocation to category of mastoid surgery altered if necessary. The series included children whose initial surgery was completed elsewhere, potentially with different indications, but MEP results are only reported after surgeries completed at the study site because of availability of prospectively recorded operative data.

Children were assessed with tympanometry in both ears at post‐operative clinic visits. Otoscopic examination was completed by the surgeon. Tympanometry was completed by a pediatric audiologist using a conforming probe tip and a Grason Stadler tympanometer (Grason‐Stadler Inc., Eden Prairie, MN, USA) at a frequency of 266 Hz. Tympanometer function was calibrated annually. The value of MEP pressure was determined at peak compliance. All post‐operative tympanometry findings were included for analysis. Results were categorized into Type a (compliance peak ≥ 100 daPa), Type c ( ≤ 100 daPa), Type b (flat trace with no compliance peak) as suggested by Jerger [ 15 ]. Results were also categorized into normal and abnormal using more rigorously determined age‐specific reference ranges (compliance peak −95 to 23 daPa at age 6–13 years, and −44 to 11 daPa at age 14–80 years) [ 8 ]. If tympanometry could not be completed because of an incomplete seal (e.g., perforation, tympanostomy tube, wide meatoplasty) or lack of patient cooperation, the tympanogram was categorized as not available (NA). MEP values were recorded from contralateral ears without cholesteatoma that were otoscopically normal at pre‐operative clinic visits.

As a variable number of tympanometric measures was available according to length of follow up, a final measure analysis, using only the most recent value, was completed to provide one MEP measure per ear. To allow analysis of the entire dataset, including all measures of MEP after all surgeries, and control for the known increase in MEP with age [ 8 ] and potential confounding effects of cholesteatoma severity or numerator of surgery (i.e., whether first, second, third, or fourth operation) on MEP, linear mixed effects modeling was used. This avoids the limitation of using the last surgery per ear (which excludes prior surgeries, potentially of a different category, with subsequent recurrence) and the limitation of using only one MEP measure per ear (which may not be representative of typical pressure). Non‐parametric tests were used to compare MEP between groups because of skewed distribution of MEP values. Analysis was completed using R version 4.3.3 on RStudio‐2024.04.2–764.

471 children were included with a mean age of 11.4 years (range: 1.9–17.9 years) at the first recorded surgery. 742 surgeries were completed during the study with an average of 1.6 surgeries per ear though most ears had only one surgery (mode and median = 1). Noting that some ears received prior operations elsewhere, 381 surgeries were the initial operation, 274 a second stage or revision, 75 the third surgery, 10 the fourth surgery and two were the fifth surgery. Overall, 303 (40%) surgeries were categorized as Group A (transcanal, mastoid sparing), 320 (43%) were Group B (CWU), 85 (11%) were Group C (CWD), and 34 (5%) were Group D (CWU‐BOT). There were 2983 follow‐up assessments with a median of 6 per child (range: 1–24). Tympanometry was successful on 2381 operated ears (79.8%) with a median of four per operation (range: 1–21). Type b (flat) tympanogram was present in 751 (31.5%), giving a total of 1630 MEP measurements on operated ears. Tympanometry was obtained in normal looking contralateral ears on 1388 occasions. MEP was lower in younger children in normal and operated ears, but there was no significant difference in MEP by EAONO‐JOS stage of cholesteatoma (Supplement 2 ).

Tympanometric findings from the most recent clinic assessment are shown in Table 1 . At this time point, averaging around age 16 years, MEP in operated ears (median = −65 daPa) was lower than in normal contralateral ears (median = 5 daPa) (no statistical testing as unbalanced contribution of one or two ears per child to the analysis). Subset analysis using data from final visit in which MEP was measurable on both sides (i.e., the operative and normal contralateral ear) was completed to allow a matched pair analysis. In this select group of 149 patients, median MEP was lower in the operative ear (median = −37 daPa; Wilcoxon signed‐rank test: p = 2.58 × 10 −7 ). Type a tympanogram was present in 89% of normal ears but only 38% of ears operated on for cholesteatoma. When applying more recently derived lower limits of normal for MEP [ 8 ], 78% of normal ears had pressure above the lower limit of normal compared with 29% of operated ears. Figure 1 shows box plots for distribution of final MEP for each of the four groups of mastoid surgery. There was no strong statistical evidence of a difference in MEP by any type of mastoid surgery (Kruskal–Wallis rank sum test: p = 0.396). Although Group D (CWU‐BOT) has median MEP closest to normal at −31 daPa, there are only 16 ears with measurable MEP in this group. As shown in Table 1 , normal Type a tympanograms were found in around 40% of ears after surgery categorized as Group A, B, and D with Type c, Type b and NA each around 20%. The proportion of operative ears in surgical Groups A, B, and D with MEP above the lower limits of normal [ 8 ] is around 30% (29%–34%). Group C, the modified radical mastoidectomy group, differs from the other surgical Groups, having a higher proportion of unmeasurable MEP, and when measurable, the proportion with normal pressure and Type a is smaller still.

When including age at first surgery, category of mastoid surgery (Groups A to D), the numerator of the surgery (i.e., from first to fifth operation), severity of cholesteatoma (using EAONO‐JOS stage), age at MEP measurement, and simultaneous tympanometric status of the contralateral ear, in LMEM it is evident from Table 2 that the variables having the strongest statistical evidence of an effect on MEP are age and the status of the contralateral ear. For example, MEP after surgery is predicted to be 76 daPa lower when the contralateral ear has a Type c tympanogram (average MEP in the operative ear = −125 daPa (95% CI: −173 to −76.4 daPa) with contralateral Type a tympanogram and −201 daPa (−252 to −50.8) with contralateral Type c tympanogram; p < 0.001). When results are averaged over the levels of the categorical variables in the model (numerator of surgery, EAONO‐JOS stage, contralateral tympanogram type), there is no difference in MEP between any of the types of mastoid surgery: Group A −166 daPa (−216 to −117); Group B −167 daPa (215 to −118); Group C −164 daPa (−214 to −115); Group D −146 daPa (−203 to −89). Likelihood ratio tests were used to compare the relative importance of each predictor, showing that removal of status of contralateral ear from the model has the strongest statistical effect on the fit of the model ( p = 2.2 × 10 −16 ). Age at test was strongly associated with MEP ( p = 6.3 × 10 −7 ), more so than age at first surgery ( p = 0.001). Removal of category of mastoid surgery does not have a strong statistical effect on the fit of the model ( p = 0.7008). Removal of EAONO‐JOS stage ( p = 0.5059) and numerator of surgery ( p = 0.07797) also have no strong statistical effect on the model. In summary, MEP increases with age and is lower when MEP is low in the contralateral ear, but MEP appears not to be dependent upon the type of mastoid surgery or cholesteatoma severity.

MEP homeostasis helps maintain normal tympanic membrane structure and function, with negative pressure contributing to tympanic membrane retraction and development of primary acquired, and potentially recurrent, cholesteatoma. This large prospective study of children with primary acquired cholesteatoma shows that tympanometric MEP remains lower than normal in a small majority of ears post‐operatively, regardless of surgical management of the mastoid. Although MEP increases with age and normalizes after age 6 in contralateral ears, average MEP remains below normal at all ages post‐surgery. A strong correlation was found between low MEP in the operative ear and low MEP in contralateral ears. Although tympanoplasty success may correlate with health of the contralateral ear [ 16 ], these findings do not necessarily imply that MEP status of the contralateral ear would predict risk of recurrent cholesteatoma: events causing low MEP in the normal ear, such as upper respiratory tract infection, would likely also reduce MEP in the operative ear simultaneously. The objective of this study was to investigate contradictory hypotheses which propose that different surgical strategies for mastoid management should create more normal MEP homeostasis. As outlined in the introduction, these include restoration or obliteration of mastoid mucosal function, preservation or removal of mastoid mucosa, and surgery to enlarge or reduce the air‐volume reservoir [ 2 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ]. Such mechanistic reasoning (Level 5 evidence [ 17 ]) is not supported by the absence of any difference in MEP between different categories of mastoid surgery using the Level 3 evidence provided by this study. The implication of this conclusion is that such hypotheses should not be used to influence surgical decision making in children with cholesteatoma. The unpredictable behavior of tympanomastoid mucosa may explain some variability in outcome and discordance with hypothetical mechanisms. In the author's experience, ventilation pathways often scar closed. The mastoid only remains well‐aerated in around half of CWU tympanomastoidectomy surgeries [ 11 ]. Attempted prevention of these scars with esterified hyaluronic acid lamina was unsuccessful, without improving MEP or recurrence risk [ 18 ]. Whether the tympanomastoid system remains aerated or not is thought to influence middle ear gas exchange and MEP [ 19 ] but even if well‐aerated, modeling shows that the mastoid would not act as a significant buffer for changes in middle ear pressure [ 20 , 21 , 22 ]. Clinical outcomes should instead guide surgical strategy. So for example, a transcanal approach may be favored to reduce post‐operative morbidity [ 23 ] and a canal wall up tympanomastoidectomy or canal wall down with obliteration to provide access for more extensive disease without leaving the child with cavity management problems. Mastoid obliteration has been advocated to reduce the risk of recurrent cholesteatoma [ 14 , 24 ] although, when controlling for risk factors for recurrence including age, cholesteatoma severity, and certain syndromes, type of mastoid surgery does not appear to alter the risk of recurrence [ 13 ]. That observation is consistent with these findings, that post‐operative MEP is independent of type of surgery. Research in progress on this dataset suggests that recurrence most commonly arises in the attic, regardless of initial site of cholesteatoma origin. If confirmed, selective attic dysventilation explains the pathogenesis better than negative MEP [ 25 , 26 ]. Even after obliteration, recurrence can grow into the obliterated attic. Considering these observations, the possibility of patulous Eustachian dysfunction [ 3 ], and the finding that post‐operative MEP was normal in around one third of cases, the findings of this study cannot safely be extrapolated to assume that attempting to relieve negative pressure with Eustachian tube balloon dilatation would prevent pediatric cholesteatoma recurrence.

Eustachian tube function could not be measured in this cohort, so any differences in MEP from patulous or obstructive dysfunction between surgical categories was not assessed. Allocation to category of mastoid surgery was based on extent and severity of disease. Possibly, factors that influenced cholesteatoma extent and severity would also influence MEP post‐operatively regardless of type of surgical intervention. Although MLEM analysis controlled for age and cholesteatoma stage, the paucity of aggressive cholesteatoma in the mastoid sparing group and small cholesteatomas in the mastoid elimination groups limit the power of this analysis. A relatively small number was allocated to Group D (CWU‐BOT) because of greater post‐operative morbidity found by the author with this technique and experience that recurrence rates were not so different from other approaches [ 13 ]. Data on MEP from centers with a larger CWU‐BOT practice would be of interest. MEP was not measurable in all ears on all clinic visits and in some ears this was a consistent outcome. Some contributing factors are associated with middle ear disease, such as atelectasis, otitis media with effusion or tympanostomy tube. Tympanometry failed more often after CWD, likely due to large meatoplasty. It is unclear if findings apply to unmeasurable ears. Accuracy of tympanometry as a measure of MEP has been questioned. Using a synthetic model for calibration, there was linear correlation between tympanometric and actual measures of pressure below −46 daPa [ 27 ], making tympanometry appropriate for confirming MEP below the lower limit of normal pressure at all ages [ 8 ]. However when modeling very small middle ear volumes (total 0.85 mL), tympanometry reported pressures that were approximately twice as low as large volumes. This suggests tympanometry may over‐estimate negative pressure when the mastoid is not well‐ventilated and may explain lower MEP in Group C. Other methods of measuring MEP have included intra‐operative use of pressure transducers in the mastoid [ 19 ], and trans‐tympanic needles connected to a manometer [ 28 ] but these invasive methods are not practical for repeated measures over years in a large series of children. Of note, the latter study reported MEP in 14 ears post‐surgery of which six (43%) had normal pressure, a similar proportion to this study. CWD and CWU cases were included in that study but difference or similarity between the two groups of surgery was not described.

After pediatric cholesteatoma surgery, tympanometric measures of MEP remain lower than normal, regardless of surgical approach to management of the mastoid. MEP was similar after transcanal surgery which preserves the mastoid, CWU tympanomastoidectomy which aims to increase mastoid volume, and CWD or mastoid obliteration surgery which remove any contribution of the mastoid to MEP homeostasis, although sample size was small for the latter. These findings do not support using unproven mechanism‐based hypotheses to guide surgical approach.
